papers.authors: Rogers Kaliisa, Crina Damşa, Jan Arild Dolonen, Malcolm Langford, Runar Hilleren Lie, Terje Kristian Lian Thoresen, Richard Nesnass, Krishna Siddharth Rajasekaran
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Students & Learners
papers.abstract: This demo presents TeamLearn, a multimodal collaboration analytics dashboard designed to facilitate reflection and provide feedback on developing group artifacts during long- term collaborative problem-solving projects. By integrating meetings, documents, and collaboration experience analytics, the dashboard offers visualisations that help groups monitor participation, task progress, and collaboration dynamics. Developed through a design-based research process, the TeamLearn dashboard provides structured opportunities for reflective dialogue. The demo will showcase the dashboard’s core features and illustrate how it can be integrated into collaborative project activities.

papers.title: Dialogue, Design, and Reflect: Partnering with Teachers to Transform Education
papers.authors: Gayithri Jayathirtha, Joanna Goode, Gail Chapman, Taghrid Elmeligui, Elaine Griggs, Tangela Crocker, John Ottina, Don Yanek, Jennifer Parr
papers.design_stakeholders: High School Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: Teachers have the potential to be transformational agents of change. And yet, fewer accounts from practice illuminate the process of teachers becoming transformational agents. In this paper, we present a composite counterstory developed with six high school teachers to demonstrate how they and their colleagues evolved as transformational intellectuals through their participation in professional activities over the years, including inquiry -based teacher professional development (PD) sessions, co- designing a justice -oriented computing program, and reflecting on their experiences . Drawing from thematic qualitative analysis of video recordings of five reflective sessions with teachers at the end of a three -year-long codesign work, we answer: How did teachers develop as transformational intellectuals through co- designing a justice -oriented computing curriculum alongside inquiry- based professional development and reflective practice? The counterstory highlights themes that emerged from the analysis, showing that teachers developed trusted relationships , agency, and solidarity through critical historical analysis and reflectivity.

papers.title: Integrating Augmented Reality and Product Design in Makerspaces
papers.authors: Dejan Trencevski, Jina Kang, Vishal Sachdev, Aric Rindfleisch
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Undergraduate / Graduate Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: This study aims to explore the affordances of augmented reality technologies (AR) to facilitate studentsʼ product design processes in a business course. We analyze the affordances of AR in the context of a product design activity in an undergraduate classroom. The course is held in a Makerspace lab at a university campus, and it requires students to conceptualize, design, prototype, manufacture, and market new products by using 3D computer -aided design (CAD) software and 3D printing. Our study illuminates that although CAD allows students to visualize and manipulate digitally manufactured 3D objects on a 2D computer monitor surface, it does not allow them to visualize and manipulate those 3D objects in 3D space. However, AR does afford visualization and mani pulation of digitally manufactured 3D objects in 3D space which is why we investigated how do interactions with 3D models in AR impact product design processes for students.

papers.title: Supporting Classroom Orchestration and Collaborative Programming with Jupyter Analytics
papers.authors: Zhenyu Cai, Richard Lee Davis, Roland Tormey, Pierre Dillenbourg
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Students & Learners
papers.abstract: Jupyter notebooks have been widely adopted in STEM courses that have programming or data science integrated. Jupyter Analytics, a learning analytics system, has been built to provide teachers with visibility into student activity. In combination with its existing functions as an awareness and reflection tool, this demo illustrates how the new code- sharing feature can address the real needs of both instructors and learners within Jupyter notebooks. Specifically, we discuss its potential value in two use cases: (1) supporting teachers in orchestrating live-coding lectures, and (2) helping students merge and synchronize work in collaborative programming. This covers two common pedagogical contexts in higher education: teacher-led lectures and student-centered active learning environments with group projects or collaborative sessions.

papers.title: Teacher as Designers: Using Robotics to Integrate Computational Thinking and Science
papers.authors: Michael Cassidy, Debra Bernstein, Jennifer Cross, Karen Mutch-Jones
papers.design_stakeholders: Middle School Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: This study examines how middle school science teachers designed and implemented robotics-based units that integrated computational thinking (CT) practices following a professional development (PD) program positioning them as curriculum designers. Drawing on Waterman et al.’s (2020) and Coenraad et al.’s (2022) integration frameworks and the project’s CT framework (Bernstein et al., 2025 ), we analyzed teacher interviews, implementation logs, lesson plans, and student materials from six teachers across twelve units. Findings show that teachers implemented CT at multiple integration levels, engaging students in algorithm design, decomposition, abstraction, pattern recognition, and data practices. Teachers explored CT practices to establish foundational understanding, enhanced CT– science connections through scaffolds, and guided students to exhibit disciplinary ideas through programmable mode ls and extend understanding by collecting and analyzing data. These findings illustrate how positioning teachers as informed designers supports CT-integrated science curricula. Importance Computational technologies are essential for problem solving and collaboration in both professional and personal contexts (NRC, 2014). In STEM fields, these technologies have transformed practice through abstraction, algorithms, decomposition, modeling, simulation, and data analysis enabled by computing (Puttick et al., 2024; Weintrop et al., 2016). Preparing students to participate in such transformations requires the development of computational thinking (CT) practices, defined as “solving problems, designing systems, and understanding human behavior, by drawing on the concepts fundamental to computer science” (Wing, 2006, p. 33). Such preparation positions students to become producers, not merely consumers, of computational solutions. Yet despite growing calls to integrate CT into K –12 science classrooms, teachers face persistent challenges in designing learning tasks where CT meaningfully supports science learning (Cassidy & Puttick , 2022). Teachers are rarely positioned as designers of curricula that combine science, engineering, and computing (Margot & Kettler, 2019), leaving limited evidence on how to support them in planning, adapting, and enacting such curricula in authentic ways (Lee et al., 2020). Conceptual framework Computational Thinking (CT) Prior research offers important frameworks for conceptualizing CT integration. For example, Waterman et al. (2020) introduced a continuum of CT integration in science education, distinguishing between levels where CT exists (CT concepts, skills, and practices already present in the lesson can be called out or elaborated upon by the teacher, often without technology use), enhances (development of additional tasks or lessons that serve to deepen the disciplinary concept while making explicit connections to relevant computing ideas), and extends (redesign or expand lessons so that computing or CT practices become central to students’ engagement with disciplinary content). More recently, Coenraad et al. (2022) added the category of exhibit, which emphasizes students’ representing science knowledge through computational models. These frameworks provide a robust lens for describing the variety of ways CT can interact with disciplinary science learning. Engaging with robotics enables learners to develop CT practices while investigating core scientific phenomena, positioning robotics as a powerful context for integrating disciplinary learning with computational problem solving (Cassidy & Puttick, 2022). Through robotics, students apply key CT practices such as problem decomposition, abstraction, algorithmic design, and iterative debugging. These activities also support engagement in core science practices, including modeling, experimentation, and data collection and analysis (e.g., Sullivan & Hefernan, 2016). For the Robots in Science project, we adopted the PRADA framework (Dong et al., 2019), which emphasizes pattern recognition, abstraction, decomposition, and algorithms. To better align with the needs of 1297 science and robotics integration, we extended PRADA by including a fifth practice, Data Practices (Weintrop et al., 2016). In our framework, pattern recognition refers to identifying similarities among and within problems. Abstraction involves stripping away unnecessary details to develop a generic solution or representing a complex system through a simplified model or visualization. Decomposition is the process of breaking down data, processes, or problems into smaller, manageable parts. Algorithm design c oncerns the creation of an ordered sequence of instructions to solve a problem or perform a task. Data practices include collecting information, analyzing it to generate insights, and representing it through graphs, charts, words, or images. Professional development for teachers-as-designers Positioning teachers as designers acknowledges their capabilities as effective curriculum developers who draw on both disciplinary knowledge and classroom expertise (Penuel & Gallagher, 2009). This approach recognizes teachers’ pedagogical knowledge, their professional judgment, and their ability to innovate in response to their unique contexts (Voogt et al., 2019). When teachers design and/or adapt their curricula and instructional practices, they put disciplinary goals, student learning needs, and classroom resources at the forefront of implementation (Puttick et al. , 2025). Professional development that supports this role emphasizes strategies such as active learning, practice- based inquiry, and collaborative design, which create opportunities for teachers to engage directly with new ideas while situating them in the realities of classroom practice (Darling -Hammond, 2017; Tucker-Raymond & Gravel, 2019). Also, time is needed to be allotted for deep play with new technologies and resources (Koehler et al., 2011). Thus, teachers’ curriculum adaptations are shaped by their wisdom of practice and responsiveness to student needs (Calabrese Barton et al., 2021).

papers.title: From Making Sense to Taking Ownership: Teachers’ Evolving Participation in AI Education Across Disciplines
papers.authors: Qiuqing Li, Daria Smyslova, Amanda Williams, Shiyan Jiang, Carolyn P. Rosé, Jie Chao
papers.design_stakeholders: Math Teachers; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This study examines how teachers’ participation evolves as they engage in learning about and implementing AI -integrated lessons. Grounded in the Community of Practice framework, this study traces teachers’ movement from peripheral understanding to central contribution within an emerging AI educator community. Findings reveal four forms of participation: disciplinary entry, reframing for disciplinary fit, recognizing the scope and fit of AI practices, and envisioning coherent student learning across courses. These findings show that sustainable AI integration begins with disciplinary anchoring and develops toward ownership and systemic coherence.

papers.title: How Teachers Learn by Designing AI-Ethics Scenarios Using an LLM-Supported Authoring Tool
papers.authors: Jeanhee Lee, Sieun Park, Yue Wang, Kyuwon Kim, Yeji Ko, Hyo-Jeong So
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Students & Learners; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: This study investigates how teachers learn by designing AI ethics scenarios using a customized LLM-supported authoring tool. Seventeen pre - and in-service teachers engaged in dilemma-based scenario design within the Learning by Design framework through int eractive dialogue with the LLM. Data from prompt logs, think- aloud sessions, surveys, interviews, and reflections revealed diverse prompting patterns. Teachers alternated between seeking guidance and generating, evaluating, and refining ideas. Through this process, they developed a deeper understanding of AI ethics, greater confidence, and more student -centered perspectives, viewing AI as a collaborative design partner. The findings suggest that iterative prompting and scenario design provide an effective pathway for teacher learning and highlight the potential of LLM-supported environments for professional growth in AI-integrated education.

papers.title: Investigating Collaborative Weaving Design as a Scaffold for AI Literacy
papers.authors: Carolyn Rose, Olivia Robinson, Melisa Orta-Martinez, Joey Huang, Kylie Peppler
papers.design_stakeholders: Undergraduate / Graduate Students; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This poster presents version 1.0 of a curriculum unit designed to expose students to machine learning concepts related to representation and reasoning, an understudied area in AI literacy. Embedded within a textile art course, this three-week pilot explores whether hands-on weaving activities scaffold or distract from AI concept acquisition. Students design weavable potholders while engaging with an AI agent that demonstrates both capabilities and limitations of large language models.

papers.title: Co-Designing Hybrid Intelligent Learning Environments: One Educator’s Journey Navigating Relationships with AI
papers.authors: Lili Yan, Jina Kang
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) have resulted in a “replacement framing” in education. Hybrid intelligence (HI) has been proposed to reframe the relationship between educators and AI as collaborative, positioning humans and AI as partners in learning. Empirically, however, little is known about the impact of the HI system on the complex ecologies of learning in K -12 classrooms. To foreground educators’ agency in shaping HI systems for learning, we partner with a group of secondary science teachers exploring the role of hybrid intelligent systems in science learning contexts. We present a case of one educator’s experience to illustrate how teachers navigated their relationship with AI during the process to co-design a hybrid learning environment based on the existing science learning simulation, HoloOrbits. Findings highlight teachers’ evolving trajectories and leadership in co- designing AI-augmented systems, which reveals how teachers negotiate forms of AI-teaming aligned with their pedagogical visions.

papers.title: Bridging Theory and Practice: A Design-Based Research Approach to Strengthening Evaluation in Science Museums
papers.authors: Kari Ross Nelson, Lisa Lundgren
papers.design_stakeholders: Educators & Practitioners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This design -based research study examines the relationship between evaluation theory and practice in science museums. Through interviews with six museum evaluators and a broader survey, researchers found that museum evaluators have minimal engagement with formal evaluation theory, relying instead on on- the-job training, templates, and practical tools. This tenuous practice -theory relationship stems from limited formal evaluation training, with most evaluators entering the field through adjacent roles rather than intentional career planning. While evaluators do reference some pragmatic frameworks, they more commonly draw from concrete resources and theories from adjacent fields such as education and psychology. This work-in-progress outlines the first phase of a multi-phase DBR project aimed at co-designing a professional learning tool that strengthens evaluation theory use among science museum evaluators. This research demonstrates how learning sciences methodologies can advance understanding of learning in informal contexts while simultaneously contributing to practice - based theory development in evaluation.

papers.title: Designing the Next Generation of Computational Modeling and Learning with AI
papers.authors: Tamar Fuhrmann, Line Have Musaeus, Ole Sejer Iversen, Paulo Blikstein
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: As generative AI rapidly transforms how humans interact with computation, it challenges the foundations of many educational technologies designed to teach coding, modeling, and computational thinking. Systems that were once built around writing or arranging code—whether block-based or text-based—now coexist with tools that generate programs through natural language. This workshop invites the learning sciences and design research community to collectively explore how educational technologies that include coding must be re-envisioned in light of these shifts. What will it mean to “code,” “debug,” or “model” when AI becomes a co-author? How might our existing environments—like MoDa, a block-based modeling platform, or text-based NetLogo simulations—need to be rethought for an era where learners reason through prompts, outputs, and model interpretation rather than syntax and structure? Our goal is to identify key design principles, challenges, and opportunities to guide the next generation of AI-powered computational learning environments. Theoretical background and significance Integrating computational thinking (CT) into science education equips students with powerful tools to explore scientific phenomena, foster deeper conceptual understanding, and engage in authentic scientific practices. The interdisciplinary potential of this work empowers students and practitioners to engage meaningfully with emerging local and global challenges (Barr et al., 2011; Weintrop et al., 2016). Existing literature identifies several core CT practices: abstraction, generalization, decomposition, algorithmic thinking, and debugging (Caeli & Yadav, 2020). Computational modeling, including agent-based modeling (ABM), has long been recognized as a valuable tool that can simultaneously support students' science learning and CT (e.g., Wilkerson et al., 2015; Musaeus et al., 2023; Musaeus et al., 2022). Recently, however, developments in Artificial Intelligence (AI) have introduced new possibilities for how learners and educators may interact with computational models (Chen et al., 2023). In the future, it may no longer be necessary to write code to create scientific computer models, putting learners in the role of collaborators with generative AI. For decades, coding has served as both a tool for learning and a language for thinking (Papert, 1980; diSessa, 2000). Block-based and text-based environments embody constructionist ideals, empowering learners to express, test, and refine ideas through computation. Yet today, this paradigm is shifting. AI’s ability to generate executable code from natural language redefines what it means to “speak computation.” As we transition from programming languages to prompting, foundational concepts—such as loops, conditions, and agents—risk becoming invisible. At the same time, new epistemic practices emerge: prompt engineering, iterative interpretation of AI outputs, and ethical reasoning about algorithmic agency. This timely workshop for the field of learning sciences demands that we rethink not only curricula, but also what fundamental concepts in programming that we still need to teach and how to design the tools themselves; how they mediate learning, distribute agency, and scaffold understanding when code is no longer the learner’s sole artifact of construction. Organizing team Line Have Musaeus leads research at the Center for Computational Thinking & Design, focusing on computing education, computational modeling, and STEM learning. Her work explores how integrating computational thinking into school subjects supports both student learning and teacher development. She co-designed CoTinker and has extensive experience organizing workshops on computing and AI in education. Tamar Fuhrmann leads research at the Transformative Learning Technologies Lab at Teachers College, Columbia University. She is a founding leader of the MoDa project, focusing on computational modeling in science education. Her work integrates STEM, AI, and constructionist approaches, and she regularly leads professional development and international collaborations. Paulo Blikstein is an Associate Professor at Columbia University and director of the Transformative Learning Technologies Lab. His research focuses on using technology to t ransform learning in STEM and AI. He founded the FabLearn program and has received major awards, including the NSF CAREER and AERA Early Career Award. Ole Sejer Iversen is a professor at Aarhus University and director of the Center for Computational Thinking & Design. His research focuses on computational empowerment, helping young people become active creators of technology. He works at the intersection of participatory design, computing education, and policy, leading large-scale international projects. Workshop goals and intended audience This workshop is designed for researchers, designers, and educators in the learning sciences, computing education, and educational technology who are exploring the future of computational learning in the age of AI. It will particularly interest those developing or studying coding-based environments—such as block-based, text-based, or modeling tools—and those investigating how generative AI transforms students’ epistemic, creative, and design practices. Participants with backgrounds in design-based research, computational modeling, or AI in education will find opportunities to share perspectives, contribute to collaborative redesign activities, and help shape a research agenda for rethinking the role of coding and modeling in AI-mediated learning environments. Outline of planned activities and facility requirements The four-hour workshop (plus one hour for lunch and coffee) will begin with an opening and framing session (20 minutes) introducing key tensions in AI-integrated coding environments. This will be followed by case study provocations (40 minutes), during which participants engage with two computational modeling environments: MoDa, a block-based agent-based modeling tool, and CoTinker, a collaborative modeling environment. Participants will explore and design models while considering how these tools might evolve as learners use AI to generate, modify, and explain models. In the collaborative design challenge (60 minutes), small groups will reimagine an educational technology that includes coding, redesigning it to integrate AI while preserving learners’ epistemic and creative engagement. This will lead into a group synthesis and discussion (40 minutes), during which participants share insights, identify emerging principles, and surface tensions, producing a poster as the group outcome. The workshop will conclude with a closing reflection (20 minutes), focusing on articulating open research questions and opportunities for future collaboration. Participation requirements Participation is open to researchers, designers, educators, and graduate students interested in computational modeling, coding education, or AI-supported learning environments. No specific technical expertise or prior experience with educational learning environments is required. We would like to support a dynamic, collaborative environment in which multiple perspectives on the redesign of coding-based educational technologies can emerge. Relationship to similar events conducted in the past Over the past several years, ISLS conferences have hosted numerous workshops and symposia exploring computational modeling, data science education, and AI-supported learning, for example, Kafai et al., 2025; Wagh et al., 2024; Fuhrmann et al., 2022; Fuhrmann et al., 2024; and McElhaney et al., 2020. These events advanced theoretical and design frameworks for integrating computational practices into science and engineering education. However, few have directly addressed the implications of generative AI for redesigning the educational technologies that include coding, particularly how block-based and text-based modeling environments must evolve when learners can construct programs through natural language. This workshop builds on that lineage but reframes the central question: not how to teach coding, but how coding itself—and the tools built around it—should be reimagined for an AI-mediated future. By convening researchers working at the intersection of computational modeling, design-based research, and AI in education, the session extends ongoing ISLS dialogues toward a new design agenda: understanding how AI reshapes the epistemic and pedagogical foundations of computational learning tools. Expected outcome and outputs The workshop will strengthen a community of practice focused on designing tools that preserve human sense- making and agency alongside AI assistance. It will generate open-ended questions that help rethink computational educational technologies in an AI-mediated context, and build a shared vocabulary around emerging hybrid practices where coding, prompting, and modeling intersect. Rather than defining what the future of coding should be, the session aims to open a dialogue on how our tools—and our field—must evolve to meet it. papers.title: The Impact of Discourse in Knowledge Building Teacher Communities on Professional Agency in Interdisciplinary Instructional Design
papers.authors: Li-Ting Tseng, Mei-Ju Chen, Huang-Yao Hong, Chao-Yu Guo
papers.design_stakeholders: K-12 Teachers
papers.abstract: This stu dy examines how discourse within a Knowledge -Building (KB) teacher community shapes professional agency in interdisciplinary instructional design. Sixty- nine teachers participated in collaborative design tasks, and their discourse was categorized i nto sharing-oriented and knowledge -building-oriented groups. Mixed- method analyses revealed a shift from exploratory sharing to knowledge -building discourse, characterized by negotiation and i ntegration of teaching strategies. Teachers’ professional agency im proved across all dimensions, particularly in positive interdependence and collective efficacy. The findings underscore the critical role of knowledge -building discourse in fostering teacher agency and supporting interdisciplinary instructional innovation.

papers.title: Creating Artifacts for Expansive Science Teaching through Art-Based Collaboration
papers.authors: Deborah Dutta, Miwa A. Takeuchi
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: The need for newer ways to enact human- nature relationships calls for educational practices to expand their boundaries of learning. Several educational initiatives have engaged in integrating arts -based practices with science learning to broaden the scope and aims of learning. However, the creation of artifacts that mediate the processes by which science educators can expand their pedagogical repertoire to engage with the emergent possibilities of arts-based practices has received less attention. This study describes collaborative processes between an artist and a pre-service teacher, Becca, which inspired her attempts to reimagine her teaching aims and practices, as part of a summer camp research –design partnership on a community urban farm. The study highlights how the evolution of pedagogical artifacts through collaborations made space for emergent learning anchored in embodied experiences.

papers.abstract: Research-practice partnerships (RPPs) and design- based implementation research (DBIR) emphasize co-design with stakeholders, yet approaches for collaborative data analysis remain underdeveloped. This paper examines how design approaches can scaffold quali tative and quantitative inquiry for diverse partners in co-analysis processes. We present two working examples: the TRACE Project, which developed a community -driven taxonomy of arts program outcomes through collaborative classification with 26 community arts organizations, and the Whole Child Analytics Project (WCAP), which employed AI -assisted reflection tools to measure college and career readiness competencies through teacher and student co-design in a large, urban school district. Through these cases, we illustrate methods for creating spaces that afford meaningful engagement from all partners while honoring multiple perspectives, voices, and worldviews in the analysis process.

papers.abstract: We present the design of a partnership among science education practitioners, molecular biologists , and high school biology teachers. Using Lave and Wenger’s (1991) construct of legitimate peripheral participation, we demonstrate how the partnership created conditions for meaningful engagement in the specialized epistemic and cultural practices of structural molecular biology. The SHAPE MATTERS project facilitated an iterative professional learning program in which 24 teachers and their students engaged in increasingly sophisticated approximations of modeling practices ––from using physical and computational molecular models to presenting molecular stories. The team also developed a continuum of molecular modeling for high school biology. The structural biologists ensured disciplinary authenticity; science educators provided pedagogical knowledge. Our case presents a proof-of- concept for a practical approach that moves beyond generalized enactments of scientific practice by grounding teaching and learning in specific research contexts, supporting teachers and their students to develop experience in nuanced enactments of scientific modeling.

papers.title: Designing for Affective Equity in Partnerships
papers.authors: Blanca Gamez-Djokic
papers.design_stakeholders: Educators & Practitioners; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Research-practice partnerships (RPPs) have become central to the learning sciences as infrastructures for addressing educational challenges. While much scholarship emphasizes their design principles and effectiveness, less attention has been paid to the affective life of partnerships. This paper advances a conceptual argument that RPPs function as pedagogical sites of affectivity. They not only rely on dispositions such as trust, humility, or perseverance but also cultivate, normalize, and organize which affective orientations become legitimate forms of participation. I call this the ontological goodness of RPPs – the assumption that collaboration is inherently moral and transformative which imbues partnerships with affective demands that shape who can participate fully and on what terms. Reframing purpose as an affective terrain highlights a hidden curriculum of partnership and raises new learning and design questions: what would it mean to design RPPs for affective equity where multiple orientations are legible and recognized as legitimate forms of participation?

papers.title: Distributed Cognition Meets Culturally Relevant Pedagogy: A Cognitive Journey Through Board Game Redesign
papers.authors: Shuvo Chowdhury Rahul, Beaumie Kim, Reyhaneh Bastani, Jerremie Clyde, Alex Poppendorf, Bogusia Gierus
papers.design_stakeholders: Students & Learners
papers.abstract: This paper presents a qualitative thematic analysis of a focal group engaged in redesigning a board game in junior high school. Grounded in distributed cognition and culturally relevant pedagogy, we identify four interconnected themes that explain how collaborative sense-making accelerates: (1) Digital and cultural tools as semiotic resources; (2) Peer dynamics and unequal influence; (3) Distributed leadership and participation; (4) Dialogic facilitation and k nowledge construction. The findings enhance our understanding of how a group’s cognitive engagement becomes most productive when material, symbolic, and cultural resources converge, highlighting the fragile yet transformative role of cultural relevance in equitable, design-based learning.

papers.title: From Enrichment to Essential: The Value of the Arts in Education and Learning
papers.authors: Harper Staples, Anna Keune, Sinyoung Kim, Kristiina Kumpulainen, Naomi Thompson, Mary DiCioccio

papers.abstract: This symposium positions the arts as central to learning. Arts -based education has been shown to cultivate creativity, empathy, and cultural awareness, while supporting academic achievement and well -being. Despite this , the arts remain marginalized in curricula, with funding cuts and narrow evaluation frameworks obscuring their value. Responding to calls to advance knowledge on learning in and through the arts, this symposium seeks to demonstrate approaches to valuing the arts through six contributions that show methodological and theoretical innovations, alongside purposeful partnerships, that capture the value of arts-based education. The symposium will include roundtable presentations within a participatory fishbowl and co-creation of a tangible emotional cartography of insights, advancing future directions for evidencing the value of arts-based education through research, policy, and practice. Symposium overview The arts are central to how we understand learning and knowing and are therefore crucial to the learning sciences (Halverson & Sawyer, 2022). The arts have long been recognized as powerful contexts for cultivating empathy, creativity, and cultural awareness (Eisner, 200 2; Venkatesh et al., 2023) . The arts have also supported academic achievement and positively impacted mental health and wellness (Peppler et al., 2014; Fancourt & Finn, 2019). Unlike other domains, arts -based education engages learners in per sonally meaningful experiences that link identity, community, and imagination (Halverson et al., 2023; Peppler et al., 2023). Importantly, these experiences are also democratic: arts -based education can nurture the pluralism and inclusivity that underpin participatory societies. This value has been affirmed globally; UNESCO, for example, through its 2022 MONDIACULT declaration, emphasizes that culture and the arts are integral to human development, well -being, and creativity, forming the foundation for respect and openness to otherness , which are all skills essential for 21st- century life (UNESCO, 2024). Despite its crucial role, arts -based education often remains marginal in curricula, positioned as “auxiliary” rather than central (Halverson, Saplan & Martin, 2024, p. 300). One challenge lies in evaluating the impact of arts-based education. As Jindal-Snape et al. (2018, p.60) note, attempts to measure “a range of aesthetic and emotive experiences which themselves defy categorization” risk reducing the richness of artistic engagement and obscuring its intrinsic value, namely, its distinctive capacity to “i lluminate our inner lives and enrich our emotional world” (Mowlah et al., 2014, p.4). Compounding this issue, even amid increasing global attention, there remains uncertainty about how the arts are and should be connected to education and assessment (Fleming, Bresler & O’Toole, 2015, p. 1). To address these gaps, more robust and responsive ways of articulating arts -based education, its role, and its purposes are essential. Building on this prior work crystallizes an important opportunity: To articulate the value of arts- based education through approaches that can capture both the distinctive ‘ ways of knowing ’ (Wright, 2012) and the “examples of success that are possible” in arts -based educat ion (Halverson et al., 2024, p. 310), while also 2375 foregrounding the broader social outcomes it enables . Making sense of artistic and cultural experiences requires situated, learner-centered, and embodied perspectives in which “senses, cognition, and emotions are developed together” (Chemi & Du, 2022, pp. 6- 7). This socio -cultural and situative approach to learning through the arts strongly resonates with the learning sciences (Halverson & Peppler, 2018). As such, t he learning sciences are uniquely positioned to advance richer understandings of both how the arts -based approaches shape what can be learned through the arts and how this learning can be made visible and valued. papers.title: Co-design as Transformative Pedagogical Spaces: what zooming out teaches us about learning to co-design together
papers.authors: Michael Chang, Areej Mawasi, Angel Osorio Pizarro, Thomas M. Philip, Amani Rohana, Jool Farra
papers.design_stakeholders: Math Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: This symposium brings together Learning Scientists and practitioners engaged in co- design practices embedded in diverse traditions (participatory design, human- centered design, youth participatory action research, design- based implementation research, and research practice partnerships) across diverse geographies. In different ways, these collections of papers challenge two artificially imposed constraints on how many co- design spaces are (a) designed, as short, condensed, irregular, or infrequent activities, and (b) studied, as analysis primarily focused on the interactions happening within the formal co -design activities themselves. By zooming out temporally and analytically, we make visible co- design processes that are deeply context-dependent, relational, political, and ethical practices, ones that researchers and participants construct a nd hone together over longer units of time. Through our collective discussions, we show how co- design spaces are unique spaces of being, doing, and becoming, for researchers and participants alike. Objective of the session In recent years, collaborative design has emerged in the learning sciences as a key method supporting the development of learning artifacts (Yoon et al., 2016; Gomez et al., 2018). Like other design-oriented disciplines, co-design in the learning sciences seeks to surface participants’ lived experiences and needs to directly inform the design of some learning artifact. Unlike other design-oriented disciplines, co-design in the learning sciences has focused on the relational, social, and dynamic learning processes that occur within co-design spaces (Mawasi et al., 2023; Penuel, 2019; Philip et al., 2022). This burgeoning line of research from the learning sciences complicates how we design, analyze, and assess co -design spaces, particularly when time constraints often necessitate that these co -design sessions occur over short or infrequent periods. Extrapolating concrete design decisions from co- design spaces can be exceptionally difficult given the fluidity, tensions, and outright contradictions that emerge ( Chang & Philip, 2025). Here, rather than narrowly conceptualizing the telos of co- design spaces as surfacing fixed designs, we build on Rogoff’s conceptualization of “learning as a process of transformation of participation” (1994) and argue that co- design spaces must be understood as sites where participants and researchers dynamically learn to co -design together. In this way, we understand co- design as a deeply context-dependent, relational, political, and ethical practice that researchers and participants construct and hone together; design decisions thus emerge as an ever-evolving byproduct of these practices (Bang & Vossoughi, 2016; Vossoughi et al., 2021). Past work in the learning sciences offers several starting points for exploring co-design spaces as sites of mutual learning about co-design itself. McKercher (2020) argues that building conditions for co-design workshops 2274 require intentional power sharing, relationship and trust building, and creating safe spaces for participants. The relational nature of co -design spaces presents a key challenge, as co -design engagements (in practice) typically occur over a short, condensed time period (10s of hours). Such tensions, even when unintended, raise important questions for the Learning Sciences community regarding what co-design entails and how to educate participants and researchers in co-design. Prior work has begun to conceptualize co-design as co-researching with participants and youth (e.g., Clark et al., 2022), while educating learners about the research process. While past work gestures towards the deep relational work that happens in co- design processes, our understanding of how those relational processes unfold is often constrained by two artificially imposed constraints on how many co- design spaces are (a) desi gned, as short, condensed, irregular, or infrequent activities, and (b) studied, as analysis primarily focused on the interactions happening within the formal co -design activities themselves. This symposium brings together five projects that seek to zoom out from these constraints in different ways and conceptualize co -design as a pedagogical space that generates educational possibilities (Freire, 1976) for transformation and shifts in interactions, dynamics, relations, roles, and knowledge, while positioning both researchers and participants as learners of co-design. The projects offered here are hardly the only projects in the learning sciences that thoughtfully challenge those constraints; we seek to make a humble contribution by bringing together a highly diverse group of co-design projects that engage with those constraints and possibilities in creative ways. By exploring these constraints and possibilities, we collectively explore different approaches we have taken in exploring this argument, by focusing on five examples of what we consider a form of co-design research work. Across these projects, we take care to highlight the conditions for co- design, describing the process of mutual becoming and what is transformed in the process, emerging issues in the co-design process (e.g., relational trust, context, power, shifts, ideologies, axiologies), and the tensions or possibilities between desired outcomes and what was eventually achieved. This focus enables us to make the following contributions: (1) We bridge between various co-design projects in the field to recognize the multiplicity of approaches to co-design, and to refine our conceptualization of co-design. (2) We outline key challenges for conceptualizing co -design spaces in the learning sciences for both technology-mediated environments and work with educators, practitioners, and learners using participatory methods. (3) We examine the kind of learning co-design environments afford to participants and, researchers in their collaborative learning process. (4) We examine the ways co -design can be a potential space for creative and constructive exploration and deconstruction and construction of ideas, among participants and researchers with no necessarily defined outcomes needing to emerge - enabling possibilities for critical thinking, liberatory education, and fluid outcomes that create new possibilities for groups and that could be similar to group work in psychology treatments. Overall, the symposium provides guidance on addressing co- design not only as a methodological approach, but also as a learning environment design that enables diverse possibilities for learning for both participants and researchers. Each of the five projects here identifies different ways to zoom out from the typical frames used to study co-design spaces, thereby illustrating different ways that researchers and/or participants learn from each other in ways that enrich the co -design process: (1) Chang et al. zoom out from one -off co-design intensives to show how researchers and youth participants negotiate the aims of co- designing AI-for-education tools over a three -year period. (2) Mawasi et al. zoom out from the formal co- design activities and show how a team of researchers/designers, themselves operating from the margins, learn from each other in order to create co- design spaces around ethical AI that respond to the political contexts of Arab/Palestinian youth. (3) Romero & Lee zoom out from simplified descriptions of participant needs to demonstrate how decision junctures during long-term co -design processes, both big and small, shape how researchers and participants participate in co- designing math and computer science curriculum. (4) Takeuchi et al. zoom out from recent history to demonstrate how researchers and participants learn to attune themselves to the agency and teachings of the Land through mutual learning and imagining, spanning approximately 12,000 years of land stewardship by indigenous communities. (5) Ehrenfeld et al. zoom out from the seemingly convenient touchpoints between researcher and academic during co-design and demonstrate how mismatched rhythms of co-design create pedagogical and ethical tensions when researchers partner with math educators. Collectively, these projects illustrate heterogeneity in co -design research enactment across geographies, topics, and methodological choices of design- based research, and demonstrate how co -design can serve as a productive framework across disciplines, including AI in Education, Mathematics Education, and STEM Education. Together, these contributions assert the need for teams t o co-design for co- design—to continually 2275 examine and refine the very processes and relationships that make co-design possible. As a final point, to illustrate our conceptualization of co-design across these five papers, we share Figure 1, an example of tatreez, Palestinian embroidery art. The art of tatreez , as described by the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO, 2021), particularly among women, is an intergenerational and sociocultural practice whose symbols and motifs (e.g., birds, trees, flowers, and places ) carry knowledge, stories, memories, and epistemologies. It has been, and continues to be, widely practiced within Palestinian communities. By “zooming out,” the front and reverse offer two vantage points on a single, entangled practice in which the product carries the process: some makers keep the reverse deliberately neat; others show thread paths and revisions. As Palestinian women engage in tatreez , they enact several choices while being intentional about what they are creating; they often do so in community and in circles, talking with one another. Like co -design, tatreez interweaves structure and improvisation, and ties knowledge to land, relations, and stories. Made collectively—in circles and conversation—the practice is both what is created -and-process itself, a space for care and knowledge-building. Figure 1 Tatreez Tatreez (noun and verb) as co -design: form-and-process as one entangled practice. The patterned front and the reverse—whether kept deliberately neat or showing thread paths —are complementary views of the same iterative making. As in co -design, meaning emerges through interwoven structure and improvisation, situated relations, ties to land, and storytelling. Handmade by Areej Mawasi. Overview of the symposium A key theme of this year’s International Society of the Learning Sciences (ISLS) conference centers on creating learning experiences that “partner with purpose” with the communities we design with and for. However, such intentions for purposeful partnership require a nuanced understanding of the educational ecologies that shape research–practice partnerships and collaborative design efforts. These intentions also call for an acknowledgment of the resources, capacities, and constraints at play for both communities and researchers across the various cycles of design and partnership—such as temporality, sociocultural and political contexts, histories, relational dynamics, and the lived experiences of participants (e.g., Bang & Vossoughi, 2016; Ehrenfeld & Stengel, 2025; Mawasi et al., 2023). While we expect this symposium to be held entirely in person at the conference venue, we will intentionally build in the option for remote participation by presenters to accommodate emergent circumstances that affect presenters’ ability to travel. papers.title: Teacher Autonomy in Organized Informal Learning
papers.authors: Racheli Davies, Nadav Ehrenfeld
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Researchers often refer to teacher autonomy in either how they learn in professional development or how they make choices about what and how to teach. These two areas of teacher autonomy are usually studied separately, which we argue is problematic, and thus bring them together. We focus on a 4- day summer workshop where teachers were given unusually high levels of freedom to set their own goals and learning. By looking at the choices teachers made we explore what it means for teachers to exercise different kinds of professional judgment. We draw on Boote’s (2006) idea of professional discretion, illustrating how some relied on existing materials and organized them for their classrooms, while others developed new materials that addressed local student needs. By examining these choices, we highlight potential opportunities for how teacher autonomy can be supported to foster more innovative professional practice. Objective Research on teacher autonomy is fragmented across two main bodies of research. The first stems from teacher education and professional development literature and deals with different forms of teacher autonomy or its absence in their learning (e.g., Horn & Garner, 2022; Kennedy, 2019; Lefstein et al., 2020), and the second stems from policy and curriculum investigations and deals with teachers’ freedom to make choices about what they teach and how (e.g., Hong & Youngs, 2016; Pearson & Moomaw, 2005). The gap between these two bodies of knowledge is problematic because autonomy cannot be “provided” without proper support to realize it (Hargreaves, 2016; Marco et al., 2025). For these reasons, we position this paper and investigation at this intersection, in line with scholars who bridge that gap (e.g., Boote, 2006; Severance et al., 2016). From this stance, we argue that teacher curricular autonomy is both necessary and requires support for teachers to exercise it. Our overarching goal, in both practice and research, echoes Boote’s (2006) argument that “developing innovative professional discretion should be the long- term goal of teacher development and curriculum policy” (p. 468). Towards this goal, in this exploratory paper we first define teacher curricular autonomy as teachers’ capacity to make curricular choices and to implement them (Hong & Youngs, 2016; Pearson & Moomaw, 2005). Then, we present Boote’s conceptualization of three levels of teacher professional discretion marked by increased competence: procedural, substantive, and innovative professional discretion. Finally, we illustrate teacher choices in a professional development setting we call organized informal learning, distinguished from more typical PD activities by the high level of autonomy teachers are provided with. Within the context of this 4-day-long summer workshop, we ask, What type of choices did participants make about the structure and content of the curricular materials they developed? What choices did participants make about their own activity within the PD? We explore these questions with an eye towards providing fertile ground for future research and professional development designed to develop teachers’ ability to exercise innovative professional discretion. Within such top-down PD activities, teachers are seen as passive consumers of knowledge, with little to no influence o ver what they will learn and how (Lefstein et al., 2020). In contrast, current notions of quality teacher PD emphasize collaborative reflection on problems of teaching raised by teachers and situated in their everyday practice (e.g., Darling-Hammond et al., 2017; Ehrenfeld, 2025). papers.title: Bridging Gaps: Participatory Design as a Tool for Social Justice in Education
papers.authors: Tugce Aldemir, Rogers Kaliisa, Rotem Israel-Fishelson, Nitzan Koren, Emily Oswald, Paulo Blikstein, Danielle P. Espino, Seung B. Lee, Eric R. Hamilton
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: This symposium explores how participatory design (PD) can disrupt the "one -size- fits-all" approach by fostering equitable, responsive, and contextually relevant practices in the learning sciences. Leveraging PD to address systemic inequities, the symposium showcases studies that empower immigrant teens as co -designers and learners in crafting experiences for informed civic participation, employ micro-genetic analyses to examine equitable partnerships among diverse stakeholders, explore curriculum co -design in resource-constrained settings to enhance teacher agency, utilise cooperative inquiry for designing inclusive schools for LGBTQIA+ students, and use of participatory design to advance inclusiveness in an international network of informal STEM clubs. This symposium illustrates how PD can change educational spaces and advance the Learning Sciences' commitment to social justice, ethical collaboration, and inclusive practices through case studies, methodological insights, and interactive discussions. Overview and significance Participatory design (PD) is increasingly recognised for its potential to advance equity and inclusion in education. Rooted in collaboration, PD engages learners, educators, researchers, and community members in co -designing learning environments, tools, a nd systems that address diverse experiences and needs. The Learning Sciences community has long emphasised the creation of ethical, inclusive practices that disrupt systemic inequities and foster equitable learning opportunities (e.g., Bang & Vossoughi, 2016; Gomez et al., 2021). However, despite the continued focus on inclusion within the learning sciences, empirical evidence and case studies that highlight how marginalised and underrepresented voices are included remain limited. This symposium aligns with the learning sciences’ commitment to social justice by showcasing how PD can challenge the "one -size-fits-all" approach to education. PD provides a pathway to address systemic challenges such as language barriers, identity affirmation, and power dynamics, creating equitable and contextually relevant educational practices (DiSalvo & DiSalvo, 2014; Hoadley, 2017; Vossoughi, 2020). PD fosters inclusive practices that support all stakeholders, particularly in diverse, resource-constrained settings, by including marginalised voices. The symposium presents five contributions that cover a wide range of educational contexts, including empowering immigrant teens as co-designers and learners in crafting civic engagement experiences, using micro- genetic analysis to explore teacher- stakeholder collaborations in curriculum co- design, designing inclusive schools for LGBTQIA+ youth through Cooperative Inquiry, and how participatory design can advance inclusiveness in an international network of informal STEM clubs. These cases illustrate how PD can adapt to real-world constraints, enhance agency, and create educational spaces aligning with the learning sciences' commitment to diversity, equity, and inclusion. Through interactive presentations, participants will engage with empirical, methodological, and theoretical insights, fostering discussions that bridge research and practice. This symposium not only advances the understanding of PD as a tool for social justice but also invites the learning 2365 sciences community to reimagine educational research and design for a more equitable future, echoing calls for ethical and inclusive practices (Gomez et al., 2021; Uttamchandani et al., 2020). papers.title: Designing for Resilience as Preparation for Challenging STEM Tasks
papers.authors: Tanmay Sinha, Naseema Beevi, Ria Gavin Dias
papers.design_stakeholders: K-12 Teachers; Youth & Adolescents
papers.abstract: We designed a novel instructional package targeting distinct facets of mental and emotional resilience for thirty -nine primary school students as preparation for a collaborative design challenge in a Singaporean science classroom. Our mental resilience package nudged sensemaking around growth mindset by having students make predictions on myths, and offered vicarious learning opportunities for everyone to evaluate peer quotations of reframing failure. Our emotional resilience package used contrasting cases complemented with expressive writing to help students discern the usefulness of positive and negative emotions in learning. Several data sources – including students’ reflections, their descriptions of enacted resilience behaviors, and observable measures of science learning – showed evidence that this work may have already begun planting seeds for normalizing failure and persevering emotionally through setbacks.

papers.design_stakeholders: Undergraduate / Graduate Students
papers.abstract: As AI increasingly enters the classroom, what changes when students collaborate with algorithms instead of peers? We analyzed 36 undergraduate students learning graph theory through peer collaboration (n=24) or AI assistance (n=12), using discourse analysis to identify interaction patterns shaping learning outcomes. Results suggest a collaboration quality divide: high-quality peer interactions generated curiosity and engagement that AI couldn’t match, yet low-quality peer interactions performed worse than AI across dimensions. AI showed a paradoxical pattern, building confidence in knowledge while reducing curiosity and deeper engagement. Interaction quality emerged from dynamic patterns rather than individual traits, with early discourse markers predicting outcomes. Students treated AI as a transactional information source despite its collaborative design, revealing fundamental differences in human versus algorithmic engagement. Our findings suggest AI in education need not replace peer learning but can recognize struggle and support both peer and AI interactions toward productive learning experiences.

papers.title: Stories, Futures and Histories: Co-design Routines to Center Community Knowledge for Environmental Education in India
papers.authors: Gautam Bisht, Vishesh Kumar, Pankaj Dev, Jyoti Tiwari, Ankit Bhatt, Lata Upreti, Kiran Pant

papers.abstract: Centering co-design as a site of social justice, we analyze a collaboration between learning scientists and local teachers from a non-profit organization in the Himalayan region of Uttarakhand, India. We ask, what design routines support the emergence of c ommunity-driven ideas for ecological education, and how do they build on each other to deepen cultural, imaginative, and historical engagement? Data for this paper comes from the initial phase of collaboration, which consisted of six online meetings, each two hour long. We conducted thematic analysis along to identify three interconnected routines: (i) autecology narratives surfaced ecological connections grounded in community and personal rituals, (ii) speculative futuring opened imaginative engagement with communication, technology, and markets; and (iii) interactions with community elders supported the development of critical historicity. Together, these routines illustrate a co -design approach which fosters collective sense -making integrating cultural, imaginative, and historical dimensions of community life .

Yet students strategically managed affect and negotiated epistemic ideals, thereby transforming affective tensions into opportunities for shared understanding.

papers.title: Comparing High School Students’ Collaborative Discourse in Idea-Centered and Procedure-Based Technology-Supported Scientific PBL
papers.authors: Ying-Tien Wu, Ti-Cheng Tsai, Li-Jen Wang
papers.design_stakeholders: High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This quasi -experimental study compared collaborative discourse between idea - centered and procedure-based science PBL among 61 Taiwanese high school students over 12- week. Using a hierarchical coding framework, student contributions were coded into three levels—information sharing, knowledge construction, and knowledge building—at individual and group levels. Results showed idea-centered PBL significantly increased knowledge - building discourse (73.6% vs. 34%) and promoted idea diversification and synthesis. These findings suggest that epistemological framing embedded in platform design shapes students' collaborative discourse.

papers.title: Calling, Collecting, and Transformation: Playful Artifacts as Pivots for Joint Activity and Game Design in a Collaborative VR Design Studio
papers.authors: Heliya Ahmadi, Xingxing Xie, Dylan Paré
papers.design_stakeholders: Undergraduate / Graduate Students; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This paper examines how artifacts and environmental features mediate collaborative design in immersive VR. In a six- week VR collaborative studio, six designers co- created an LGBTQ+ mini-golf game. By triangulating video recordings with reflective journals, we found a stimulus -to-transformation design process that emerged from the perceptual noticing of collectibles, evolving into shared ideation and transforming game mechanics. Situated within activity theory, the study contributes process -oriented methods for researching collaborative VR design.

papers.title: Leveraging Generative AI for Iteration in Undergraduate Design
papers.authors: Inés Álvarez-Icaza, Claudia Susana López Cruz, Martha Elena Núñez López, Griselda Esthela
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Undergraduate / Graduate Students; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Training designers requires not only technical skills, but also the ability to think critically, creatively, and strategically. Design applications powered by Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) are emerging every day, hence educators are concerned about the development of students’ creative abilities. The project is a pedagogical experience mediated by a GenAI tool, the ‘DIAgent’. Through a dynamic interaction between initial sketches, guiding questions, and automated feedback provided by the tool, students iterate their proposals, considering key variables such as form, usability, ergonomics, materials, and technology. This study is conducted with a mixed-method approach as an exploratory study to assess the creative abilities of a sample of 103 undergraduate students after the intervention. This paper presents the tool and the application protocol to be applied in six different design classes as the study’s first phase results, leading to a better understanding of how to redefine the students’ desi gn process.

papers.title: Towards Teachers-AI Collaboration for Professional Development in Learning Design
papers.authors: Shatha N. Alkhasawneh, Davinia Hernández-Leo
papers.design_stakeholders: K-12 Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This study examines how Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) can enhance learning design (LD) by exploring stakeholders’ preferences for five conceptual GenAI -based conversational agent functions —Authoring Assistant, Inspiration Hub, Design Feedback, Possibility Engine, and Ethics Guardian—adapted from the GenAI Speculative Functions Framework for LD. Proposed for the TRAILS teacher professional development platform, these functions target underexplored early phases of LD. Using a convergent mixed-methods design, 56 participants evaluated these functions, their support needs across design phases, and related opportunities and concerns. Findings reveal a two- pillar demand: creative inspiration, prioritized in the Investigation phase through the Inspiration Hub, and drafting efficiency, prioritized in the Authoring phase through the Authoring Assistant. The analysis revealed role- dependent value: experienced practitioners favored generative and creativity -oriented functions, while prospective teachers emp hasized diagnostic and feedback support. The Ethics Guardian emerged as an essential ambient safeguard. The study offers practical guidance for integrating human- centered GenAI into teacher professional development platforms and human-AI collaboration in LD.

papers.authors: Wenli Chen, Lishan Zheng, Xuanyu Chen, Mavis Ho

papers.abstract: This study examines how individual preparation (IP) before collaboration influences learners’ verbal communication during collaborative learning. By comparing immediate collaboration with collaboration following IP, this study employed the Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA) to investigate the differences in learners’ verbal discourse patterns. The results indicate that while IP before collaboration fosters more structured communication, marked by enhanced task coordination and responsiveness, it reduces spontaneous negotiation. The findings suggest a trade-off between structured preparedness and flexibility, with implications for optimizing collaborative learning design.

This study evaluates COALESCE through its application in designing an AI-assisted lesson-planning tool. Our findings show how deep educator involvement supports trust, ownership, and domain-specific improvements in AI-generated content. We discuss implications for participatory AI design and offer a replicable model for context-aware, educator-aligned innovation.

papers.authors: Joe Curnow, Rishi Krishnamoorthy, Ali R. Blake, Gerardo Villagrán Becerra, Sophia Thraya, Arundhati Velamur, Ishita Pradhan, Tatiana Becerra, Mahati Kopparla

We ask, ‘how might the Learning Sciences rearticulate theories of learning that serve life rather than capital accumulation, and racialized and gendered hierarchy?’

papers.authors: Tong Li, Joshua A. Fisher, Younkyung Hong
papers.design_stakeholders: Elementary / Early Childhood Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: As schools become culturally diverse, integrating students' cultural backgrounds into teaching practices is essential. Culturally Responsive Teaching (CRT) has emerged as a critical focus in professional development (PD) for educators. However, many PD programs inadequately train teachers in CRT, resulting in superficial cultural integration. This exploratory study investigates the impact of educational game design workshops on promoting CRT, positioning teachers as serious game designers. Nine elementary mathematics teachers participated in a workshop that involved designing culturally responsive educational games. Through thematic analysis of interview data, findings reveal that game design fosters teachers’ empathy and understanding of students' cultural contexts, enabling the incorporation of diverse cultural elements into their teaching. Challenges identified include cultural gaps and limited design skills. The study highlights the potential of collaborative game design in enhancing CRT, suggesting that hands-on, creative PD approaches can deepen teachers’ cultural awareness and instructional practices.

papers.authors: Andrew Estrada Phuong, Ashley Quiterio, Da’Von L. McCune, David W. Jackson, Fan Huang, Finn Goehrig, Ifeoma Nwogu, Kellyann Ramdath, Marcelo Worsley, Megan Butler, Noemi Waight, Stacy M. Scheuneman, Stanley M. Lo

papers.abstract: This symposium critically examines existing educational research methodologies through the intersection of Quantitative Critical Theory (QuantCrit) and Learning Sciences frameworks. Drawing inspiration from Garcia et al.’s (2018) QuantCrit principles—which emphasize the centrality of racism, the non-neutrality of numbers, and the importance of critically examining research categories—the symposium addresses how quantitative data can reinforce deficit-oriented narratives and underscores the necessity of incorporating and centering marginalized voices. Paper 1 explores how young adolescents from historically minoritized backgrounds engage with and resist artificial intelligence technologies within community contexts. Paper 2 presents findings from a Differential Item Functioning (DIF) analysis of an identity survey in a university biology setting, revealing how survey items may exhibit bias despite intentions toward equity. Paper 3 utilizes (post)qualitative inquiry to deconstruct power dynamics, question normative knowledge production, and center diverse voices, highlighting the co-constitutive relationships between researchers, participants, and environments.

papers.title: Amplifying Teacher Voice in Collaborative Research

papers.abstract: Research practice partnerships (RPPs) are a promising approach to transforming educational practice by amplifying the voices of teachers. This approach is especially powerful for disrupting educational inequities by positioning local actors as experts to generate solutions and take action. This cross-case study examines how engaging mathematics and science teachers in collaborative inquiry gave voice to teachers’ experiences as they sought to transform their instruction for equity and justice. Informed by process and practice theory perspectives, we describe how the social arrangement of cowriting supported teacher researchers in generating new concepts and practices for equitable and just instruction. We identify four specific practices - gaining clarity and consensus on equity for STEM instruction, generating representations, thinking through example cases, and cycles of feedback and accountability. Together, these practices enabled teachers to contribute to knowledge generation by advancing theory on instructional practice for justice-oriented practice through experimentation and analysis of teaching practice.

These findings illuminate how practical measures and their iterative use in Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) cycles create opportunities for teachers to hone their equitable noticing within a collaborative professional learning context. This work contributes to teacher education by identifying interpretive practice as a promising focus for fostering equity-oriented teaching.

papers.title: How Students Ground Mathematics Through Distributed Gestures: Designing Computer-Supported Collaborative Embodied Learning
papers.authors: Chaeyeon Kim, Fangli Xia, Joel P. Beier, Michael I. Swart, Kelsey E. Schenck, Mitchell J. Nathan
papers.design_stakeholders: High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: We explored how students interact with a computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) system for embodied learning in geometry. With The Hidden Village-Online (THV-O), fifteen high school students (six dyads, one triad) used movements to construct directed actions that depict geometry transformations collaboratively. THV-O is a web-based CSCL video game that uses a motion-capture to detect players’ movements, save movements they create, and play those created by their peers. By observing dyads’ co-design processes and semi-structured reflections, researchers found two important shortcomings in the design of THV-O for embodied learning: (1) players experienced difficulty in conveying geometric transformations through poses, which could hinder their ability to represent generalizable properties of space and shape; and (2) players faced challenges in jointly co-constructing a single mathematical object, limiting their ability to collaborate actively and develop shared mathematical ideas. We offer guidelines for an improved design of embodied collaborative reasoning and learning.

papers.title: Designing Curricula for an Uncertain World: A Critical Action Learning Approach
papers.authors: Chandan Dasgupta, Preeti Raman, Renato Carvalho, Hannie A. Gijlers, James D. Slotta
papers.design_stakeholders: Middle School Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Middle School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: In this paper, we focus on engaging student educational designers in critical action learning and design. While ongoing efforts have investigated how to build capacity amongst schoolteachers, we argue for building capacity amongst student educational designers who will be engaged in designing resources for schoolteachers and students. This research builds on theories of critical pedagogy and critical action learning. We follow a design-based research approach to iteratively design a critical action learning toolbox that can be used to foster a generation of designers capable of producing educational technologies that prioritize equity and social responsibility. Findings suggest that adopting a layered approach – CALE researcher/educator (Layer 0), student educational designer (Layer 1), and schoolteacher (Layer 2) – provide the required reflective space to design curricula using critical action learning approach. Scaffolds such as designing a collective problem case and emergent mirrors are important constituents in this reflective space.

papers.title: Learning from Failure Through Game Testing Feedback in Virtual Collaborative Design
papers.authors: Shulong Yan, Yu Xia
papers.design_stakeholders: Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This study investigates how learning from failure can be supported through game design feedback activities in a virtual collaborative environment. Through analyzing video recordings of three checkpoint sessions in a two-week virtual game design camp with nine youth participants (ages 8-13), we identified six feedback styles and examined how designers responded to feedback. Our findings reveal that game design feedback in virtual environments transcends traditional linear relationships, forming a complex discursive relationship among testers, designers, and game artifacts. Screen sharing emerged as a crucial boundary object, facilitating communication and transforming traditional critique sessions into collaborative learning experiences. Facilitators played vital roles by modeling playfulness, vulnerability, and productive failure responses. The study demonstrates that successful virtual design feedback requires thoughtfully curated environments that balance structured facilitation with playful engagement. These findings have implications for design education in virtual settings and suggest new approaches for supporting learning from failure in collaborative contexts.

papers.title: Fostering Inclusive Practices in Educational Policy Reform
papers.authors: Dian Mawene, Elizabeth Schrader

papers.abstract: In this paper, we examine how a group of diverse stakeholders in a predominantly White school district expanded their practice of inclusion through an intentional co-design process. The Aleph School District (ASD) in New England, U.S., co-designed a protocol for addressing discrimination and harassment, a persistent concern affecting historically marginalized students with and without disabilities. The school district partnered with the local university and employed the Learning Lab intervention (Bal et al., 2016; 2018), an inclusive, process-oriented methodology to enable the local stakeholders most impacted the chance to better understand and address their concerns. Our analysis of data suggests that, in addition to producing a needed and useful protocol, this process expanded authentic inclusion of student voice in the school district. Further, we identify practices that fostered meaningful inclusion within the Learning Lab and tangible and intangible outcomes that extended beyond the Learning Lab space.

Using the Learning at the Boundaries framework, we analyze design team meetings, teacher feedback, and co-designed curricular materials. Our findings highlight the roles of boundary spanners, practices, and objects in bridging gaps among stakeholders and fostering sustainable collaboration. This research contributes to the learning sciences by documenting effective processes for organizational learning, emphasizing the importance of structured co-design in educational improvement.

papers.title: Using the Conjecture Map for Designing an Anti-Racist Teacher Professional Development Intervention
papers.authors: S. Sushil, Sherice N. Clarke, Katherine Dennis, Ung-Sang Lee
papers.design_stakeholders: K-12 Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Educators & Practitioners; Undergraduate / Graduate Students; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Conjecture maps have long been considered instrumental in systematizing and clarifying various design and theoretical conjectures in design-based research. However, beyond enhancing design-based research, there is opportunity to clarify how the conjecture map may be used to design an intervention itself. Following the backward design logic from curricular and instructional planning, we outline here a process followed to design the first iteration of a multi-year anti-racist teacher professional development intervention that articulated the high-level conjecture, outcomes, mediating processes, and embodiments, in that order. We also present our current conjecture map and invite other researchers and practitioners to engage with in the pursuit of more effective designs for anti-racist teacher learning.
